---
title: "Module 6 — Cost, Latency, and Caching"
subtitle: "Day 3, hours 4–5 · theory, then the lab"
---

> **Never trade quality you aren't measuring for cost you are.**

LLM applications are the first mainstream software whose marginal cost per request
is large enough to bankrupt a feature, and whose latency is dominated by a
component you do not control. This module makes both engineerable — and every
optimisation is executed against Module 5's harness, which is why it comes second.

# Theory

## 1. Meter first. Optimise second.

The pricing model is simple — input tokens × rate + output tokens × rate, output
typically 3–5× input, cached input at a steep discount, batch at about half. What
makes it dangerous is the multiplication.

- **Conversation cost compounds.** Every turn resends the window, so turn *n* costs
  roughly *n* × the average turn's input. Murshid's six-turn conversation costs
  about 3× the naive single-turn estimate.
- **The forecast is four numbers multiplied**, each with an error bar: conversations
  per day × turns × tokens per turn × rate. Multiply the error bars too, and present
  a range.
- **Meter before optimising.** The `Usage` object every adapter surfaces (Module 1's
  foresight) flows into a per-request cost record — route, model id, prompt version,
  input/cached/output tokens, computed cost.

The whole price calculation is six lines, from
`src/murshid/observability/cost.py`:

```python
def price_of(self, model_id: str, usage) -> float:
    p = self._prices.for_model(model_id)
    fresh_in = max(usage.input_tokens - usage.cached_input_tokens, 0)
    return (
        fresh_in * p.input_per_mtok
        + usage.cached_input_tokens * p.cached_input_per_mtok
        + usage.output_tokens * p.output_per_mtok
    ) / 1_000_000
```

Three rates, not one, and the middle term is the entire subject of §3. Note
`fresh_in`: providers report `input_tokens` as the **total**, with
`cached_input_tokens` a subset of it. Bill the full input at the full rate *and* the
cached portion again at the cached rate and you have double-counted — a meter that
overstates cost makes caching look like it saved more than it did, which is exactly
the direction a cost report must not be wrong in. The `max(..., 0)` is defensive: a
provider that reports more cached tokens than input tokens is misbehaving, and a
negative price would be worse than a wrong one.

`self._prices.for_model(model_id)` looks the rate up by the **concrete** model id
the response carried, not by the alias that was requested. When a fallback hop
serves a request, it is priced as the model that actually answered.

```bash
make replay-before        # 200 conversations, metered, nothing optimised
```

```
200 conversations | cost/conv: 4.07 halalas | p50 turn 181ms | p95 conversation 1152ms
by intent (spend): faq 92% | service 6% | guard 1% | router 1%
by stage:  faq_handler 752.4 | service_workflow 45.9 | input_guard 8.7 | router 7.4
```

::: {.callout-important}

```bash
jq -s 'group_by(.intent) | map({intent: .[0].intent, halalas: (map(.cost_halalas)|add)})' \
   logs/llm_cost_before.jsonl
```

One JSON object per line is why `jq` is the analytics tool here. Optimising before

:::

## 2. Latency anatomy

Total latency = **TTFT** (network + queueing + prompt processing, roughly
proportional to *input* length) + **generation** (output tokens × time per token,
linear in *output* length).

| What moves TTFT | What moves generation |
|---|---|
| shorter prompts | shorter outputs — instruct for concision, `max_tokens` as backstop |
| prompt caching (a cached prefix is not reprocessed) | faster or smaller models |
| a geographically closer endpoint | speculative decoding, where the stack offers it |
| less-loaded models; on vLLM, batch pressure and chunked prefill | nothing retroactively — which is why streaming matters |

**Tails, not averages.** p95 and p99 are where provider queueing spikes, retries
(each one a full round trip) and cold caches live. The user experience is the
tail's, which is why every benchmark table in this course reports p50 *and* p95.

**A latency budget is a design artefact:** guards 0.1 ms + 35 ms, router ~50 ms,
handler TTFT ≤ 1 s, full answer ≤ 5 s p95 — written down and measured per stage, so
a regression names its stage instead of starting an investigation.

## 3. Provider prompt caching: the free 50–90%

Providers cache the *processed prefix* and charge cached input at a fraction of the
rate, cutting TTFT with it. The engineering content is **prefix discipline**.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    subgraph P["CACHEABLE PREFIX — byte-stable across every request"]
      S1[versioned system prompt]
      S2[service directory]
      S3[tool schemas]
    end
    subgraph V["VOLATILE TAIL — per conversation"]
      V1[windowed history]
      V2[this turn]
      V3["today's date, if it belongs anywhere"]
    end
    P --> V
    style P fill:#e8f4ea,stroke:#3c8d5a,stroke-width:3px
    style V fill:#fdf3e3,stroke:#c78b2c
```

**Stable content first, volatile content last.** One dynamic byte early in the
prompt invalidates everything after it. The classic self-inflicted wound is a
courtesy: a current-date-and-time line at the top of the system prompt.

`answer_faq.v4` has exactly that line. `v5` is the same prompt with the date moved
into the tail. Diff them, then look at the numbers:

| Prompt version | Prompt-cache share | Cost per conversation |
|---|---|---|
| `answer_faq.v4` — timestamp at the top | 55% | 4.07 halalas |
| `answer_faq.v5` — timestamp in the tail | [72%]{.measured} | [2.98 halalas]{.measured} (−27%) |

**Verify, do not assume.** `usage.cached_input_tokens` — plumbed through since
Module 1 — is the proof. Same request twice; the second shows most of the input at
the cached rate and roughly half the TTFT.

Two boundaries worth knowing: caches are TTL-bounded and have a *minimum cacheable
length* (the course gateway models 1024 tokens, like real providers), and they are
scoped so tenants cannot read each other's cached content. A cache hit changes your
bill, not the trust model.

## 4. Response caching: exact, then semantic

**Exact caching** is safe and boring: key = hash(model id, prompt version, rendered
prompt, parameters); value = the response; TTL by content class. Where it shines is
deterministic sub-calls — router verdicts, guard classifier verdicts, judge
verdicts in the harness.

A key that omits the prompt version serves yesterday's behaviour after today's
deploy. Ours does not:

```python
@staticmethod
def exact_key(model_id: str, prompt_version: str, rendered: str, params: dict) -> str:
    blob = json.dumps(
        [model_id, prompt_version, rendered, params], sort_keys=True, ensure_ascii=False
    )
    return "exact:" + hashlib.sha256(blob.encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()
```

Four inputs, and each one is something that changes the answer: the concrete model,
the prompt version, the fully rendered text, and the sampling parameters. Drop any
one and the cache starts lying — drop `prompt_version` and today's deploy keeps
serving yesterday's behaviour, silently, until someone notices the fix did not
take. `sort_keys=True` makes the key stable regardless of dict ordering;
`ensure_ascii=False` keeps Arabic as Arabic so two identical questions hash
identically.

**Semantic caching** embeds the query and serves a cached answer above a similarity
threshold. This is a *quality trade* and the module treats it with the suspicion
one deserves.

### Reading the two tiers

```python
def get(self, *, scope: CacheScope, query: str, exact_key: str) -> tuple[Any, str] | None:
    self.stats.lookups += 1
    raw = self._backend.get(exact_key)
    if raw is not None:
        self.stats.exact_hits += 1
        return json.loads(raw), "exact"

    if not (self.semantic_enabled and scope.semantic_eligible):
        return None                          # the whole safety argument, in one line

    index = f"sem:{scope.language}:{scope.intent}"
    vector = embed(query)
    best: SemanticEntry | None = None
    best_score = 0.0
    now = time.time()
    for entry in self._semantic.get(index, []):
        if now - entry.stored_at > self._ttl:
            continue
        score = cosine(vector, entry.vector)
        if score > best_score:
            best, best_score = entry, score
    if best is not None and best_score >= self.threshold_for(scope.language):
        self.stats.semantic_hits += 1
        return json.loads(best.payload), "semantic"
    if best is not None:
        self.stats.near_scores.append(round(best_score, 3))
    return None
```

- **Exact first, always.** It is a hash lookup; if it hits, no embedding is
  computed and no threshold is consulted. The expensive, risky tier only runs when
  the safe one missed.
- **`scope.semantic_eligible` gates the entire second tier**, and it is a property,
  not a condition written at the call site:

  ```python
  @property
  def semantic_eligible(self) -> bool:
      return not self.personalised and self.intent == "faq"
  ```

  Personalised content is excluded *by construction*. There is no code path where a
  caller can opt a personalised answer into the semantic tier, because the decision
  does not live at the call site where someone might one day "temporarily" invert
  it. That is the difference between a cost optimisation and a data-protection
  incident.
- **The index key includes language and intent**, so an Arabic FAQ answer can never
  be served for an English service question. Scoping narrows what a wrong hit could
  even be.
- **`threshold_for(scope.language)`** — the threshold is per language, which is
  what lets Arabic sit at 0.92 while English sits at 0.90. A single global threshold
  cannot express the asymmetry the near-miss suite measured.
- **`stats.near_scores` records the best *miss*.** That list is where `closest
  non-hits: [0.918, 0.909, 0.908]` comes from, and it is the only reason the lab can
  say how much margin the shipped threshold actually has. A cache that only counts
  hits cannot tell you how close it came to a wrong one.

::: {.callout-warning}
## "How do I renew my licence?" and "How do I cancel my licence?" are not the same question

They embed uncomfortably close. A naive threshold serves one as the other.

Discipline: high thresholds tuned on data and never guessed; scope keys that
include **language, intent and personalisation status**; only impersonal FAQ
content is ever eligible — anything conditioned on session state is excluded *by
construction*, not by a condition somebody might later edit.
:::

```bash
make eval-cache        # 12 near-miss pairs, bilingual
```

| Thresholds | Wrong hits | Note |
|---|---|---|
| en 0.90 / ar 0.92 — shipped | **0/12** | closest non-hits on the replay: 0.918, 0.909, 0.908 |
| en 0.85 / ar 0.85 | 1/12 | the Arabic "my record" / "my son's record" pair fires |
| en 0.75 / ar 0.75 | 5/12 | renew/cancel in both languages |

**Arabic needs a *higher* threshold than English, not a lower one.** Arabic spelling
variants of the same question score ~0.94 while English paraphrases score ~0.87, so
Arabic sits closer to its own near-misses. That asymmetry was measured, not assumed
— and it is the kind of finding a near-miss suite exists to produce.

**Honest metrics: hit rate *and* wrong-hit rate**, per scope. The pairing rule from
Module 4 has an exact analogue here. A 40% hit rate with one wrong hit per thousand
is not a saving for a government assistant.

## 5. Routing, cascades, and the break-even

**Routing by predicted difficulty is the single biggest cost lever** in assistant
workloads — and a routing change is a *quality* change, so it is eval-gated like a
prompt change.

Which is exactly what happened. The first routing table saved 91% and failed the
gate:

```
BLOCKED:
  slice:intent=faq: 94% vs baseline 100% (-6.3pt, margin 3pt)
  slice:language=ar: 95% vs baseline 100% (-5.0pt, margin 3pt)
```

The small model is fine *except* when it should be refusing: on out-of-directory
questions it stopped saying "I don't know" and started producing a plausible fee.

The reflex is to move the intent up a tier and hand the saving back. The better
answer is a **cascade** — cheap model first, escalate on a signal that is
deterministic and actually correlated with being wrong:

```python
# src/murshid/pipeline/faq.py — the SAME deterministic check the gate uses
if self._cascade_enabled and unsupported_amounts(text, directory):
    self.escalations += 1
    log.warning("cascade_escalated", from_alias=self._model_alias,
                to_alias=self._cascade_alias, reason="unsupported_amount")
    escalated = self._client.complete(
        LLMRequest(messages=messages, model_alias=self._cascade_alias, ...)
    )
```

`self.escalations` is counted, which is how `make replay-after` can report
`cascade: 0 escalations` — the claim that the cascade cost nothing on this traffic
is a measurement, not an assumption.

| Configuration | Cost/conversation | Δ | Eval verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| Baseline (`v4`, no cache, no routing) | 4.07 hal | — | green (baseline) |
| + prompt-cache discipline (`v5`) | 2.98 hal | −27% | green |
| + response cache (exact + semantic) | 1.66 hal | −59% | green, wrong hits 0/12 |
| + routing table | 0.37 hal | −91% | **BLOCKED** |
| + routing **and cascade** | **0.37 hal** | **−91%** | green, safety 100% |

The last two rows cost the same, because on this traffic the cascade escalated
**zero times**. Its insurance premium was nothing, and it is the reason the routing
table shipped.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Router or cascade? Traffic shape decides

A router pays one classification on every request. A cascade pays double only on
escalations. Which wins is a property of your traffic — and the meter is what
supplies the traffic shape. Reject model self-assessment ("was that hard?") as an
escalation signal: it is weak and sycophantic. Prefer schema-validation failures
and calibrated deterministic checks.
:::

**Self-host break-even, computed not vibed:**

```bash
make breakeven
```

Effective cost per million tokens ≈ (GPU-hour price × ops overhead) ÷ (measured
tokens/hour at *your* achievable utilisation) — using Module 2's measured throughput,
not the marketing number.

| Compared against | Crossover |
|---|---|
| the flagship tier (20.25 SAR/Mtok) | ~25% sustained utilisation |
| the cheap tier (0.90 SAR/Mtok) | never |

Both lines matter, and quoting one of them is how this arithmetic gets used
dishonestly. Residency and control usually decide *whether* self-hosting happens.
The break-even decides *what traffic* it should carry to be worth the GPUs.

## 6. Common mistakes

1. **Optimising without a meter.** A week of engineering on the 4% line item; the
   meter is one afternoon.
2. **A timestamp in the system prompt.** The entire prompt cache, invalidated by a
   courtesy.
3. **A semantic cache with no near-miss evaluation.** The renew/cancel wrong hit,
   shipping alongside a celebratory hit-rate dashboard.
4. **Cost-cutting unmeasured for quality.** The harness runs in four minutes and
   nobody ran it.
5. **Routing on model self-report.**
6. **Comparing self-host at benchmark utilisation to API at real utilisation.** The
   GPU does not run at 95%, because your traffic is diurnal.
7. **Caching personalised content.** A cost optimisation that becomes a
   data-protection incident. Personalisation status is part of the key schema, or
   the cache is a breach waiting.

### 2 · Prompt-cache discipline (10 min)

The baseline runs `answer_faq.v4`. Diff it against `v5`:

```bash
diff src/murshid/prompts/library/answer_faq/v{4,5}.md
```

```diff
-required_vars: [service_directory, now]
+required_vars: [service_directory]
-Current date and time: {now}.
-
```

One line, at the top of the prompt, changing every second. Everything after it is
uncacheable — which is the entire prefix.

```bash
make replay LABEL=s1-prefix
```

| | Prompt cache | Cost/conversation |
|---|---|---|
| `v4` — timestamp at the top | 55% | 4.07 hal |
| `v5` — timestamp in the tail | [72%]{.measured} | [2.98 hal]{.measured} (−27%) |

Verify it directly rather than trusting the aggregate: run the same request twice
and watch `cached_input_tokens` go from 0 to most of the input, with TTFT roughly
halving.

```bash
make ask Q="How do I renew my commercial licence?"    # 1413 in (0 cached)
make ask Q="How do I renew my commercial licence?"    # 1413 in (1180 cached)
```

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
### Two boundaries worth knowing

Providers only cache prefixes past a **minimum length** (the course gateway models
1024 tokens, like real ones), and caches are **TTL-bounded**, refreshed on hit. A
short system prompt never caches at all, however stable it is — which is one reason
Murshid's directory travels in the prefix rather than being fetched per request.
:::

Then run `make eval && make gate`. Green. Record the row.

### 3 · The response cache, and its safety suite (12 min)

The exact tier serves the router and guard-classifier calls; the semantic tier
serves impersonal FAQ only:

```bash
make replay LABEL=s2-cache CACHE=1 SEMANTIC=1
```

```
200 conversations | cost/conv: 1.66 halalas (−59%) | p50 turn 134ms | p95 833ms
response cache: lookups 428 | exact 210 | semantic 2 | hit rate 50% | wrong hits 0/0
                | closest non-hits [0.918, 0.909, 0.908, 0.906, 0.902]
```

Now the part that is not optional:

```bash
make eval-cache          # 12 near-miss pairs, bilingual
```

```
  ok        0.776 [en] How do I renew my commercial licen || How do I cancel my commercial lice
  ok        0.783 [ar] كيف أجدد سجلي التجاري؟ || كيف ألغي سجلي التجاري؟
  ok        0.836 [ar] كيف أجدد سجلي التجاري؟ || كيف أجدد سجل ابني التجاري؟

near-miss suite: wrong hits 0/12
```

Then break it deliberately and watch a wrong hit appear:

```bash
python scripts/eval_cache.py --threshold 0.85 --threshold-ar 0.85
## WRONG HIT 0.836 [ar] كيف أجدد سجلي التجاري؟ || كيف أجدد سجل ابني التجاري؟
```

"My commercial record" and "my *son's* commercial record" are not the same
question, and at 0.85 one citizen's answer is served to another.

::: {.callout-warning}
### The threshold decision, made with numbers instead of instinct

Look at `closest non-hits`: real replay traffic sitting at 0.918, 0.909, 0.908 —
just under the Arabic threshold of 0.92. Dropping to 0.90 converts them into hits
and leaves **0.03** of margin above the worst near-miss pair.

Take the trade or refuse it, but do it explicitly and write down which, because
that margin is the whole argument. This course refuses it: for a government
assistant a wrong hit is not a slightly worse answer.

And note the asymmetry, which is easy to get backwards: **Arabic needs a higher
threshold than English.** Arabic spelling variants of the same question score ~0.94 while
English paraphrases score ~0.87, so Arabic sits closer to its own near-misses. The
suite measured that; instinct would have got it backwards.
:::

`make eval && make gate` → green, wrong hits 0. Record the row.

### 4 · The routing table, and the correction (12 min)

Now the routing table, run against the **full** suite through the routed pipeline:

```bash
MURSHID_ROUTING_ENABLED=1 make eval LABEL=routed
make gate LABEL=routed
```

```
BLOCKED:
  slice:intent=faq: 94% vs baseline 100% (-6.3pt, margin 3pt)
  slice:language=ar: 95% vs baseline 100% (-5.0pt, margin 3pt)
```

The saving was 91%. The gate says no.

::: {.callout-important}
### This is the point of the hour

The reflex is to move `faq` up a tier and hand the saving back. Resist it for two
minutes and read what the gate actually said: the failures are all
**out-of-directory** questions. The small model is fine *except* when it should be
refusing — it stopped saying "I don't know" and started producing a plausible fee.

That is not "the small model is bad". It is a specific, cheap-to-detect condition.
:::

So detect it. Cheap model first; escalate when the answer states an amount that is
not in the directory — the **same deterministic check the gate uses**:

```bash
MURSHID_ROUTING_ENABLED=1 MURSHID_CASCADE_ENABLED=1 make eval LABEL=routed-cascade
make gate LABEL=routed-cascade
```

```
eval | 126 cases | pass 126/126 (100%) | 12.4 halalas
PASS: overall +0.0pt | worst stratum difficulty=hard +0.0pt | safety 100%
```

```bash
make replay-after
```

```
200 conversations | cost/conv: 0.37 halalas (−91%) | p50 turn 122ms | p95 687ms
cascade: 0 escalations (0% of FAQ turns paid twice)
```

**The cascade cost nothing on this traffic and bought back every point.** Its
insurance premium was zero, and it is the only reason the routing table shipped.

The transferable rule: a cascade needs an escalation signal that is cheap,
deterministic and correlated with being wrong. A schema-validation failure or a
groundedness check qualifies. "Was that hard?" does not — model self-assessment is
weak and sycophantic.

### Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `cached_input_tokens` stays 0 | a dynamic byte in the prefix, or the prefix is below the minimum cacheable length | hunt the volatile byte — `v4`'s timestamp line is the planted one |
| Hit rate 100% and everything stale | no TTL, or the replay reused one conversation | set per-class TTLs; check the replay loaded 200 rows |
| The near-miss suite shows a wrong hit | the threshold is too generous for Arabic morphology | raise the `ar` threshold specifically, and note the asymmetry |
| The routed suite fails `service` | the small model cannot hold the tool contract | that intent moves up a tier — the eval told you the table's true shape |
| p95 got worse after caching | the cache lookup was added serially to the *miss* path | a cache must be cheap to miss |
| The cascade escalates constantly | the escalation signal is too broad | it should fire on unsupported *amounts*, not on any number |

### If you finish early — the forecast

Murshid launches nationally: 250,000 conversations a day, same intent mix. Using
your *after* numbers, forecast monthly spend with a ±30% band, name the two biggest
line items, and say which single further optimisation you would fund.

One page, written for a director who will read the first paragraph and the table.
